guideTitle: Best Electric Tankless RV Water Heaters (2026)
metaTitle: Best Electric Tankless RV Water Heaters
metaDescription: Five 120V point-of-use electric tankless heaters for RV sinks and small showers, with amp draw, size and protection features explained before you buy.
expertTake: The CAMPLUX 4.5kW is the top pick for shoppers who have a dedicated high-amp circuit, since its self-modulating power control and compact body suit a sink or wet bar. The Hillhub mini is the value pick for a single handwashing tap. Anyone who expects a 30 amp RV pedestal to run one of these along with an air conditioner should skip them.
introParagraphs: An electric tankless heater has no burner, no flue and no propane line, which is exactly why RV owners keep asking about them. The heater is a small box with a heating element, a flow sensor and a safety cutout, and it turns water warm only while a tap runs.

The catch is electrical. These heaters pull serious current for a few minutes at a time, and a typical RV pedestal has little spare capacity. This guide treats electric tankless as a point-of-use tool for sinks and short rinses, and shows what each model really asks of your power system.

products.name: CAMPLUX 4.5kW 120V point-of-use tankless heater

specList.label: Use
specList.value: Under sink, wet bar, wall mount

products.description:
CAMPLUX lists this heater at 4.5kW on 120V, with a compact body about 11 inches wide and 2.5 inches tall. Its self-modulating design adjusts power input to the flow rate and temperature you ask for, which keeps the element from overheating water at a trickle. The body can be mounted at several angles in tight cabinets, which is the practical reason to pick it for a camper galley or a bath cabinet.

The electrical math matters more than any other feature. At 4,500 watts on 120 volts the heater can pull about 37 amps, which is more than a standard 30 amp RV circuit supplies. In practice that means this class of heater needs a dedicated circuit with the right breaker and wire, or a 240V service, so it is not a casual plug-in. If your rig lacks that circuit, the 3000W models below are a safer fit.

Within the right installation, ownership is simple. There is no anode, no flue and no standing pilot, and the heater has no stored water to sanitize. Keep the inlet screen clean, drain the unit before freezing, and have a licensed electrician confirm the circuit before you buy.
products.bestFor: Rigs with a dedicated high-amp circuit and a sink or wet bar to serve.
pros: Compact body mounts at multiple angles
Heats only while a tap runs
No flue, propane or stored water to maintain
cons: Draw can exceed a standard 30 amp RV circuit
Needs a dedicated, correctly wired circuit
Rated flow falls with very cold inlet water

products.name: Hillhub under-sink electric tankless mini heater
products.description:
The Hillhub is the smallest body in this lineup at about 7.9 by 2.4 by 6.4 inches, with a cast aluminum heating block and built-in dry-burn, overheat, anti-leak and water-electricity separation protection. The maker claims hot water in about three seconds, which is a statement about how fast the element reaches temperature rather than the time water takes to travel the pipe. It is designed for under sinks, vanities and counters.

The small body means the heater is a point-of-use tool, not a shower solution. Its output is lower than the CAMPLUX, so it suits handwashing and dishes more than a full rinse. That also makes it easier on the RV electrical system, since a smaller element draws fewer amps, but you must still verify the rating on the specific listing before connecting it.

Ownership is easy. Mount it close to the tap, keep the water inlet filtered and drain it before freezing, and avoid dry operation with the faucet closed. A short run of insulated hose between the heater and the tap shortens the wait.
products.bestFor: A single sink where compact size and lower current matter most.
pros: Easy to mount under a sink or vanity
cons: Hot-water time claim is a maker figure
Rating must be confirmed before wiring

products.name: 3000W 110V under-sink electric tankless heater with display
products.description:
This generic 3000W heater uses stainless steel and ABS construction with a digital LED display and an IPX4 water-resistance rating. IPX4 means it resists splashes from any direction, which is useful near a sink but does not make it safe to submerge. Multiple protection functions are listed, including overheat and dry-burn cutouts.

At 3,000 watts and about 110 to 120 volts, the heater draws roughly 25 to 27 amps, which is most of a 30 amp RV supply. That means no air conditioner, no microwave and no space heater at the same time, and it is best run from a pedestal rather than a small inverter. Next to the CAMPLUX it asks for less current, but it also delivers less temperature rise.

Ownership is basic. The LED panel gives a temperature readout, which helps you dial in a comfortable rinse, and the compact body mounts close to the tap. As with any generic listing, check the plug type and the instructions, and confirm that the wire gauge and breaker suit the load before you power it.
products.bestFor: Campers with a 30 amp pedestal who want a readout and moderate output.
pros: 3000W is manageable on a 30 amp service
Digital display shows the set temperature
cons: Still draws most of a 30 amp supply
IPX4 is splash resistance, not immersion

products.name: DOYXC 3000W 110V portable mini electric tankless heater
products.description:
The DOYXC listing names RVs among its intended uses and promotes a portable, compact design with IPX4 water resistance, leakage protection and dry-burn protection. It is a 3000W, 110V unit like the other generic heaters here, so it draws the same roughly 25 to 27 amps. The portability claim means it can be mounted or moved between locations, but it does not remove the need for a proper circuit.

The tradeoff is documentation. A listing that names RVs is not an RV certification, and the seller may be harder to reach than a major brand. It does not include the self-modulating control of the CAMPLUX, so the temperature depends on flow more than a modulating heater.

Treat it as a flexible handwashing and dish-rinsing tool. Mount it where you can reach the reset, keep a filter on the inlet and drain it before winter. Check the cord and plug rating, and keep the electrical load in mind when you plan the rest of the rig.
products.bestFor: Owners who want a portable 3000W unit marketed for RV use.
pros: Portable form can move between taps
cons: Marketing mention is not an RV certification

products.name: 3000W 110V instant under-sink electric tankless heater
products.description:
This is a basic 3000W unit aimed at bathrooms, kitchens and small spaces, with an IPX4 rating, multiple protections and a lightweight body. It is the plainest option here, with no display or modulating control called out, so it works as a simple on-demand heater for a single tap.

Its tradeoff is that it competes directly with the other 3000W units, so the choice often comes down to documentation and seller. It also shares the same current demand of about 25 to 27 amps, which leaves little spare on a 30 amp pedestal. For an owner who wants the plain version, the lower cost of entry can be the appeal.

Check the plug and cord, mount it with a way to reach the reset, drain it for winter and keep the supply filtered. Because it shares the 3000W class with two other listings, compare the instruction sheets and return terms, not the headline wattage. Treat the heater as a sink tool and keep expectations in line with a 3000W element.
products.bestFor: Buyers who want the simplest 3000W unit for one tap.
cons: Draws most of a 30 amp supply

buyingCriteria.explanation: Watts divided by volts gives amps. A 3000W unit pulls roughly 25 to 27 amps at 110 to 120 volts, and the CAMPLUX 4.5kW can pull about 37 amps. A 30 amp RV circuit cannot carry the larger unit safely, and the 3000W models leave almost nothing for other loads. Check your pedestal and breaker before you shop, not after. A quick test is to read the breaker label at the pedestal, then add the heater load to whatever else typically runs, such as a refrigerator on electric, a converter charging batteries and a coffee maker. If the total passes the breaker, the heater is the wrong tool for that site.

A heater that draws 25 amps or more needs correctly sized wire, a matching breaker and clean connections. Thin extension cords and worn plugs overheat. Many owners prefer to have an electrician add a dedicated circuit for the CAMPLUX 4.5kW rather than rely on a household cord. In a motorhome or fifth wheel with a 50 amp service, a spare breaker slot makes this practical; in a small trailer with a single 30 amp inlet, it usually is not.

Electric tankless units fire only when flow exceeds a threshold. RV faucets with low-flow aerators and a weak 12V pump may not trigger the element. Test the flow rate at the tap before mounting, and avoid aerators that cut flow below the unit minimum. If the heater clicks on and off at low flow, that is the sensor hunting at its threshold, and opening the tap a little further usually settles it.

Dry-burn, overheat and leakage protections stop an element from cooking itself or leaking current. The Hillhub lists dry-burn, overheat, anti-leak and water-electricity separation, while the 3000W units list IPX4 and similar cutouts. Treat these as baseline, and still add a GFCI-protected supply. Protection inside the heater guards the element; protection at the outlet guards the person standing at a wet sink, and they are not the same job.

A mini heater fits where a tank cannot. The Hillhub measures about 7.9 by 2.4 by 6.4 inches, and the CAMPLUX about 11 by 2.5 by 7.4 inches. Measure the cabinet, leave room for hoses and keep the body clear of splash and heat. Allow space to reach the inlet screen and any reset button without removing the unit, because a heater you cannot service gets ignored until it fails.

A small water volume still freezes. Drain the heater, disconnect hoses and store it dry before winter. Do not put antifreeze through an electric element unless the maker allows it, since the chemical can leave a film on heating parts. In a unit that sits in an unheated storage bay, bring the heater indoors for the winter if it is portable, which is one practical advantage of the DOYXC mini form.

specDecoder.meaning: Kilowatts measure the electrical power of the element. A 4.5kW heater can warm more water per minute than a 3kW one, but it draws more current.
specDecoder.watchFor: The CAMPLUX 4.5kW exceeds a standard 30 amp circuit.

specDecoder.meaning: Most RV outlets deliver 120V, which some listings call 110V. The same wattage draws the same amps at either figure within a few percent.
specDecoder.watchFor: The 3000W units use 110V in the listing, so confirm your supply.

specDecoder.meaning: A water-ingress code meaning the enclosure resists splashing from any direction. It is not a waterproof rating for submersion.
specDecoder.watchFor: The 3000W units list IPX4, so keep them out of direct spray.

specDecoder.meaning: The heater changes element power in response to flow and set temperature. It avoids overshooting at low flow.
specDecoder.watchFor: CAMPLUX states this; the basic 3000W units do not.

specDecoder.meaning: A cutout that stops the element when no water is flowing. It protects the heater, not the user.
specDecoder.watchFor: Hillhub lists it, so check the others.

howWeEvaluated.title: Electrical fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We converted each listing's wattage to amps, such as about 25 to 27 amps for the 3000W units and about 37 amps for the CAMPLUX 4.5kW. A heater that exceeds a 30 amp supply lost points unless its listing is clear about the circuit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Protection features
howWeEvaluated.description: We counted the safety features each listing states, including dry-burn, overheat, leakage and IPX4 splash resistance. The Hillhub and the 3000W units list more protections than a bare element.

howWeEvaluated.title: Size and mounting
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared body dimensions and mounting flexibility. A heater that fits under a sink without crowding the plumbing scored better, which favored the Hillhub and the CAMPLUX.

howWeEvaluated.title: Control quality
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked for a display, temperature readout or self-modulating logic. A heater that changes power with flow gives steadier water than one that is simply on or off.

howWeEvaluated.title: Seller documentation
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed how clear the listing is about wiring, plug type and instructions. Unclear documentation counted against a unit, because an electrical product needs instructions to be used safely. We also checked whether a listing shows plug type, cord length and breaker guidance, since those are the details that decide whether the installation is safe.

maintenance.why: Debris reduces flow and can stop the flow sensor from firing. A quick rinse restores operation.
A hot plug is the first warning of a loose connection at 25 amps. Replace a discolored plug.
Scale insulates the element and reduces output. Flush with a mild descaler as the maker allows.
Water trapped in the heater can crack it. Disconnect hoses and let it drain fully.
A test button confirms the outlet will trip on a fault. This matters near wet sinks.

faq.q: Can an electric tankless heater run on RV shore power?
faq.a: Only if the amp draw fits the circuit. A 3000W heater draws roughly 25 to 27 amps, which is most of a 30 amp supply, and the 4.5kW CAMPLUX can exceed it. Verify the breaker and wire.

faq.q: Can I run it from a generator?
faq.a: Only a generator with enough continuous watts can run it, and a 3000W heater needs about 3,000 watts of headroom. Most small inverter generators cannot also run other loads.

faq.q: Is electric tankless good for showers?
faq.a: Point-of-use units are better for sinks and short rinses. Showers need more output and flow than most 120V heaters deliver.
No. These heaters use 120V for the element, and a small control board runs from that supply. Check the listing for any 12V requirement.

faq.q: Why does water stay cold at low flow?
faq.a: The flow sensor needs a minimum flow to fire. Low-flow aerators and a weak pump can keep it from triggering.

faq.q: Is it safe near a sink?
faq.a: IPX4 resists splashes, but you still need a GFCI-protected outlet, a dry mounting spot and correct wiring. Follow the maker instructions, keep cords out of puddles and test the GFCI each month. If the heater or the outlet runs warm to the touch, stop using it and find the loose connection before the next trip.
